senses.gloss:
Mathurā
------------------------------------------
Rāma and कृष्ण have so deeply influenced the Hindu psyche over the last five or six millennia that no aspect or field of life of the Hindus has been left untouched by their influence. Philosophy, religion, fine-arts, architecture, sculpture, literature, मुसिच्, dancing, drama—practically every field of life, bears their impress. It is but natural that places closely associated with them became, in course of time, holy places, places of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Mathurā, a small town on the west bank of the river यमुना (in Uttar Pradesh) has been very closely associated with Lord कृष्ण’s boyhood days. Hence, this town and the area spread over 32 kms. (20 miles) around it—known as Vrajabhūmi or Vrajamaṇḍala—has been considered as extremely sacred. There are several temples here connected with the कृष्ण-cult.
The temple of Dvārakādhīśa is the biggest and worship is conducted there as per the traditions set up by वल्लभ (A. D. 1473-1531). श्रीकृष्ण जन्माष्टमी (the birthday of Śrī कृष्ण) is celebrated here on a grand scale.
The other temples are: त्रिविक्रम-नारायण-mandira, Vijayagovinda-mandira and a temple of Keśava. Patrakuṇḍa, a well near this temple, is said to be the place where baby कृष्ण’s clothes used to be washed.
Mahāvana (Mahāban) which is 14 kms. (9 miles) away, as also बलदेव at a further distance of 8 kms. (5 miles) are two more important places visited by the pilgrims.
Vanayātrā (perambulation of मथुरा) starts from the place called Viśrāmghāṭ.
The गोवर्धन hillock which कृष्ण as a child of seven years is said to have lifted up and held as an umbrella over the head, to protect the villagers from the torrential rain caused by इन्द्र, is at a distance of 26 kms. (16 miles) from मथुरा.
There is a small village nearby which has two small tanks—Rādhākuṇḍa and Kṛṣṇakuṇḍa.
Vṛndāban, another major place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, is situated at a distance of 11 kms. (7 miles) from मथुरा. There are many important temples associated with कृष्ण, here also.
Taking bath in the यमुना river on the Yamadvitīyā or Bhrātṛdvitīyā day (2nd day of the bright half of the month of Kārttika, Kārttika-śukla-dvitīyā) is considered as extremely meritorious. Such bathers are believed not to go to यमलोक or Abode of यम.
As already indicated, the entire मथुरा-वृन्दाबन् region is known as ‘Vrajamaṇḍala.’ Holikāgītas, a special kind of devotional मुसिच्, is peculiar to this region.
There are many facilities for the pilgrims like dharmaśālas (free guest houses or with very nominal charges).
There are at least 25 bathing places on the banks of the river यमुना, known as ‘ghāṭs’, like Viśrāmghāṭ, Dhruvaghāṭ, Kṛṣṇagaṅgāghāṭ, Asīkuṇḍaghāṭ and so on.
Mathurā is a very ancient city established by शत्रुघ्न, the younger brother of Śrī राम. He is said to have killed Lavaṇāsura (son of the demon मधु) and remodelled the old capital Madhupura into मथुरा. Archaeological finds at the sites near मथुरा have revealed that the town-ship must have existed even around 1000 B. C. Later on, it became a stronghold of बुद्धिस्म् and जैनिस्म्. Fa Hien (5th century A. D.) mentions that there were 20 Buddhist monasteries. Hiuen Tsang (7th century A. D.) says that 200 मोन्क्स् lived in these monasteries. But orthodox Hinduism—the भागवत Cult of Kṛṣṇabhakti or devotion to Kṛṣṇa—also was regaining its lost ground. By the 11th century, बुद्धिस्म् had practically disappeared.
During the period A. D. 1000-1700, intolerant Muslim invaders and rulers unleashed a reign of terror and destroyed many temples and Hindu religious monuments.
Almost all the Vaiṣṇava teachers and religions reformers like the followers of Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137), निम्बार्क (12th century A. D.), Svāmi Haridās (16th century A. D.), Rūpa Gosvāmi (A. D. 1493-1568) and Sanātana Gosvāmi (A. D. 1481-1558) have established their maṭhas here to spread their cult.
See also VṚNDĀBAN.
